Professional Cooking Techniques

Professional cooks get the same result every time because they understand what heat, water, fat and time do to food. This module teaches four core methods: making stock and sauces, braising tough cuts, roasting and grilling with dry heat, and frying safely. Each lesson gives you the reason behind the method, a worked example with real quantities, and the safety rules a professional kitchen follows.

Many home cooks in Nigeria build flavour with seasoning cubes. They are quick, but they add a lot of salt and every pot ends up tasting the same. Professional kitchens build flavour from **stock**: water that has been slowly simmered with bones, a few vegetables and herbs. A good stock gives body to soups, stews, rice and sauces, and it lets you control exactly how much salt goes into the food.
A pot of simmering food
A stockpot kept at a gentle simmer is the base of most professional sauces and soups.
What makes a good stock

**Bones with connective tissue.** Chicken backs, necks, wings and feet, or beef knuckle and leg bones. The connective tissue melts into gelatin, which gives the stock body. A well-made chicken stock sets like soft jelly in the fridge.
**Cold water to start.** Put the bones in cold water so that proteins rise slowly as foam and can be skimmed off. Use enough water to cover the bones by about 5 cm.
**Aromatics.** About one part vegetables to ten parts bones by weight is the classic guide. Locally that can be onion, garlic, ginger, a few thyme stems and bay leaves.
**A gentle simmer, never a hard boil.** Small bubbles should just break the surface. Hard boiling churns fat into the liquid and makes stock cloudy and greasy.
**No salt.** Stock is often reduced later. Salt added now becomes too strong after reduction. Season the final dish instead.

Worked example: a 3-litre chicken stock and what it costs
For example, Ifeoma runs a small lunch kitchen in Enugu and wants to replace seasoning cubes in her pepper soup with homemade stock.
She buys 2 kg of chicken backs, necks and feet. She rinses them, covers them with 4 litres of cold water and brings the pot slowly to a simmer.
She skims the grey foam for the first 20 minutes, then adds 200 g of aromatics (onion, garlic, ginger and thyme). That is 10% of the bone weight.
She keeps it barely simmering for 3 hours, skimming fat now and then. About a quarter of the water evaporates, so she strains out roughly 3 litres.
Her costs (approximate, prices change often): bones about N5,000, aromatics about N1,000, gas about N800. Total about N6,800.
Cost per litre: N6,800 divided by 3 = about N2,267. A 1-litre pot of pepper soup now carries about N2,267 of stock instead of cubes, and she controls the salt.
Ifeoma has a stock with real body and no added salt. She labels it with the date and uses it within 3 days from the fridge, or freezes it in 500 ml bags.

Cool stock quickly

A big hot pot cools very slowly, and bacteria grow fastest between about 5 C and 60 C. Divide stock into shallow containers, stand them in a basin of cold water with ice if you have it, and refrigerate within 2 hours. Never leave stock on the stove overnight to cool.
Reduction: concentrating flavour

**Reduction** means simmering a liquid uncovered so water evaporates and the flavour concentrates. If you reduce 1 litre of stock to 250 ml, you have removed three quarters of the water and the flavour is about four times as strong. A stock reduced until it coats the back of a spoon is called a **glaze**. A spoonful of glaze gives a stew or gravy a deep, rounded taste without adding salt.
Thickening with a roux

A **roux** is equal weights of fat and flour cooked together before liquid is added. Cooking the flour removes its raw taste. A pale roux (cooked 2 to 3 minutes) thickens strongly. A brown roux has a nutty flavour but less thickening power. As a guide, about 40 to 50 g each of butter and flour thickens 500 to 600 ml of milk to a medium sauce. Add warm liquid gradually and whisk to prevent lumps, then simmer for a few minutes so the flour finishes cooking.
The five mother sauces

French cooking groups classic sauces into five **mother sauces**: béchamel (milk thickened with roux), velouté (light stock thickened with roux), espagnole (brown stock with roux and tomato), tomato sauce, and hollandaise (egg yolks and melted butter). You do not need French dishes to use the ideas. Velouté made with chicken stock becomes a white sauce for chicken pies. A reduced brown stock improves your beef stew gravy. The principle is the same: good stock plus a controlled way of thickening.
Taste at the end
Season sauces only after reducing and thickening. Taste, add a little salt, stir, taste again. It is easy to add salt and impossible to take it out.

Braising and slow cooking tough cuts until tender
Explain why tough cuts become tender with long, moist, gentle heat
Braise goat meat, cow leg or oxtail using sear, liquid and low simmer
Use a pressure cooker safely to shorten braising time
Check doneness by texture rather than by the clock

Goat meat, cow leg, shin, oxtail and old layer chicken are full of flavour but tough. They come from muscles that worked hard, so they contain a lot of **collagen**, the connective tissue that holds muscle fibres together. Quick, hot cooking makes collagen tighten and the meat goes rubbery. Long, gentle, moist heat does the opposite: collagen slowly melts into gelatin and the meat becomes soft enough to pull apart with a fork.
A raw cut of meat
Hard-working cuts such as shin and oxtail are rich in collagen, which braising turns to tender gelatin.
What braising means

**Braising** is searing meat in a little fat, then cooking it slowly in a covered pot with liquid that comes part of the way up the meat, usually about half to two thirds. **Stewing** is similar, but the pieces are smaller and fully covered with liquid. Both rely on the same science. The liquid stays at a low simmer, well below a rolling boil, for a long time.
**Dry and season the meat.** Pat it dry with a clean cloth or paper. Wet meat steams instead of browning.
**Sear in batches.** Brown the pieces in a little hot oil without crowding the pot. Browning creates new flavour compounds on the surface.
**Soften aromatics.** Cook onions, garlic, ginger and pepper in the same pot to pick up the browned bits.
**Deglaze and add liquid.** Pour in stock or water and scrape the bottom of the pot. Add liquid until it reaches about half to two thirds of the meat.
**Cover and cook low.** Keep a lazy simmer with only occasional bubbles. Turn the meat once or twice.
**Finish the sauce.** When the meat is tender, lift it out and reduce the liquid until it is glossy and coats a spoon.

Worked example: planning a goat meat braise for a Sunday lunch

She allows 30 minutes to sear in three batches of 1 kg, so the pot is never crowded.
She adds 1.5 litres of stock, which comes about two thirds of the way up the meat in her 10-litre pot.
Her goat usually needs about 2 hours at a low simmer, and she adds 30 minutes for reducing the sauce and a 30-minute safety margin.

Pressure cookers: faster, but respect them

A pressure cooker traps steam, which raises the boiling point of the water inside to roughly 115 to 120 C. Collagen melts much faster at that temperature, so a cow leg that needs 3 hours on an open stove may be ready in well under an hour. Follow the time chart in your cooker's manual, because models differ.
Pressure cooker rules

Never fill above the maximum line, usually two thirds full, or half full for beans and foods that foam. Check that the vent and gasket are clean before every use. Never force the lid open: let the pressure drop naturally or use the release method in the manual, keeping your face and hands away from the steam. Replace a cracked or hardened gasket.
Why braised dishes taste better the next day

As a braise rests, gelatin sets and flavours spread through the meat. Many caterers braise a day ahead. If you do, cool it quickly in shallow trays, refrigerate within 2 hours, lift off the hardened fat the next day, and reheat until it is steaming hot all the way through, at least 70 C in the thickest piece.
Do not boil it hard
A hard boil squeezes moisture out of the muscle fibres and gives dry, stringy meat even when the collagen has melted. Keep the bubbles lazy.

Roasting and grilling: browning, doneness and charcoal safety
Explain how dry heat browns food and why surface moisture stops it
Roast or grill chicken and fish to a safe internal temperature using a thermometer
Rest meat correctly and estimate cooking loss
Use charcoal and gas grills without smoke, fire or carbon monoxide danger

Roasting (in an oven) and grilling (over or under direct heat, like suya or asun) are **dry-heat** methods. Hot air or radiant heat dries the surface of the food and then browns it. That brown crust is where much of the flavour comes from, and it is the reason a well-grilled fish tastes so different from a boiled one.
A roasted chicken leg
A deep brown surface comes from browning reactions, which need a dry surface and high heat.
The science of browning

When the surface of meat, fish or bread gets hot enough, sugars and proteins react to form hundreds of new flavour and colour compounds. This is called the **Maillard reaction**. It happens quickly above about 140 C. Water boils at 100 C, so a wet surface cannot get hotter than that until the water has gone. That is why professionals pat meat dry, salt it ahead so the surface dries, and never crowd a tray. Crowded pieces release steam and end up grey instead of brown.
**Dry the surface.** Pat chicken and fish dry before seasoning and oiling.
**Leave space.** Keep at least a finger's width between pieces on a tray or grill.
**Use high heat to brown, moderate heat to finish.** Thick pieces need time to cook through without burning outside.
**Add sugary marinades late.** Honey, sugar or sweet sauces burn quickly; brush them on in the last few minutes.

In a home or bakery oven, many cooks roast chicken pieces at about 190 to 200 C. Oven dials are often inaccurate, so an oven thermometer placed on the middle shelf tells you the real temperature. Turn the tray halfway through, because most ovens are hotter at the back.
Cooked through, not guessed

The only reliable way to know chicken is safely cooked is to measure the temperature in the thickest part, away from the bone. The WHO Five Keys to Safer Food advise cooking food until it reaches 70 C. A digital probe thermometer costs far less than one case of food poisoning at an event. Clear juices and no pink colour are helpful signs but they are not proof.

Resting and cooking loss

Meat loses water as it cooks, so it weighs less afterwards. This **cooking loss** matters when you are buying for a crowd. Rest meat for 5 to 10 minutes after roasting so juices settle back into the fibres instead of running onto the board. Keep it loosely covered and warm.
Worked example: measuring cooking loss on grilled chicken
For example, Chinwe in Port Harcourt sells grilled chicken quarters and wants to know how much raw chicken to buy for 40 servings of 200 g cooked meat.
She weighs 2,000 g of raw chicken quarters before grilling.
After grilling and resting, the same pieces weigh 1,500 g.
Cooking loss = 2,000 minus 1,500 = 500 g. As a percentage: 500 divided by 2,000 = 25%.
So cooked weight is 75% of raw weight. To get 40 x 200 g = 8,000 g cooked, she needs 8,000 divided by 0.75 = about 10,667 g raw.
She rounds up to 11 kg of raw chicken quarters.

Chinwe buys 11 kg instead of guessing 8 kg, so every customer gets a full 200 g portion. She repeats the test whenever she changes supplier, because the loss changes with the size and fat of the birds.

Charcoal and carbon monoxide

Burning charcoal gives off carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell that can kill. Never use a charcoal grill or coal pot inside a room, kitchen, garage or tent, even with a window open. Grill outdoors, away from doors and windows, with a bucket of sand nearby. Never pour kerosene or petrol on burning coals.
Avoid heavy charring

Fat dripping onto hot coals creates smoke and flare-ups that blacken the food. Food safety agencies advise limiting heavily charred and burnt meat. Trim excess fat, keep a cooler zone on the grill to move food to during flare-ups, and scrape off blackened bits.

Clean the grill grate while it is hot with a wire brush, then wipe it with an oiled cloth before the next use. Keep raw meat trays and cooked meat trays separate, and never put cooked suya back on the plate that held it raw.

Deep frying and shallow frying: oil temperature, oil care and fire safety
Choose a frying oil and hold it at the right temperature
Fry plantain, fish or yam evenly without greasy or burnt results
Decide when frying oil must be filtered or thrown away
Respond correctly to an oil fire

Frying is one of the most common methods in Nigerian kitchens: dodo, fried yam, akara, fried fish, fried turkey. It is also where many kitchen burns and fires start. Good frying is about one thing above all: **oil temperature**. Oil that is too cool soaks into the food and makes it greasy. Oil that is too hot burns the outside before the inside cooks, and starts to smoke and break down.
A shallow pan with food frying
Steady oil temperature is the difference between crisp, golden food and greasy or burnt food.
Deep frying and shallow frying

In **deep frying**, food is fully covered by oil, usually held at about 170 to 180 C. In **shallow frying**, the oil comes part way up the food and you turn it once, as with dodo or fish fillets. When cold food goes into hot oil, the water at its surface turns to steam and bubbles out. That outward steam is what stops oil soaking in. When the bubbling slows, the food is nearly done.

A clip-on or probe thermometer is best. Without one, drop in a 2 cm cube of bread: at roughly the right temperature for most frying it turns golden in about 60 seconds with steady bubbles. If it browns in a few seconds, the oil is too hot. If it sinks and barely bubbles, it is too cool.
Choosing and caring for oil
**Use a stable oil for deep frying.** Refined vegetable oil, groundnut oil and refined palm olein handle frying heat well. Unrefined oils and butter smoke at lower temperatures.
**Fry in small batches.** Too much food at once drops the temperature sharply and gives greasy results.
**Salt away from the oil.** Salt food after frying, over a tray, because salt falling into oil speeds up its breakdown.
**Filter after use.** Let oil cool fully, strain it through a fine sieve or cloth into a clean, dry container with a lid, and store it away from light.
**Know when to throw it away.** Discard oil that is dark, thick, smells sharp or fishy, foams heavily, or smokes at normal frying heat.
Golden, not dark brown

Starchy foods such as yam, potato and plantain form a substance called acrylamide when fried or roasted to a dark colour. Food safety agencies, including the UK Food Standards Agency, advise frying starchy foods to a golden yellow colour rather than dark brown. It also tastes better.
Worked example: is the oil still worth using?
For example, Funke in Abeokuta fries plantain and fish for a roadside lunch stand and wants to control oil cost without serving food fried in burnt oil.
She starts the week with 5 litres of vegetable oil in her deep pot. Oil costs her about N3,000 per litre (approximate).
She fries plantain first each day and fish last, because fish flavours the oil. She strains the oil every evening.
Each day she tops up about 0.5 litre lost into the food. By day 4 she has added 2 litres.
On day 4 the oil is dark, foams when fish goes in and smokes at her usual setting. She discards it.
Weekly oil cost: (5 + 2) litres x N3,000 = N21,000. Over 4 days of about 80 plates a day (320 plates), that is about N66 of oil per plate.
Funke knows her oil cost per plate and has a clear rule for discarding oil. Frying plantain before fish keeps her oil usable longer.

Any one of these signs means the oil has broken down and should not be used again.
If oil catches fire

Never pour water on burning oil: it turns to steam instantly and throws flaming oil across the room. Turn off the gas if you can reach it safely. Slide a metal lid or a damp (not dripping) fire blanket over the pot and leave it covered until fully cool. Do not carry the pot. If the fire spreads, get everyone out and call for help. A dry powder or wet chemical fire extinguisher suitable for kitchen fires is a good investment for a food business.

Prevent fires before they start. Never fill a pot more than about one third with oil. Keep the handle turned inwards. Lower food in gently with a slotted spoon instead of dropping it. Keep children out of the frying area. Never leave hot oil unattended, even for a phone call.

Customers pay for food that tastes the same every time and looks cared for. This module turns familiar dishes into standard recipes you can repeat at any quantity, teaches you to cook West African grains, legumes and proteins with precision, and shows you how to plate and present food the way hotels and good restaurants do.

Calculate the yield and cost per portion of a stew base

Ask ten Nigerian cooks how they make stew and you will get ten answers, most of them "a little of this, a little of that". That works at home. In a business it causes problems: Tuesday's stew is sweeter than Monday's, one batch is too peppery, and you never know your true cost. Professional kitchens solve this with a **standard recipe**: the same ingredients, the same weights, the same method, every time.
A chef preparing food in a kitchen
A standard recipe card lets you, or anyone you train, cook the dish the same way every time.
What goes on a standard recipe card
**Name and yield:** for example, "Tomato stew base, yield 4 kg".
**Portion size:** for example, 120 g of stew per plate.
**Ingredients by weight,** not cups or "handfuls". A kitchen scale is the most important tool in this course.
**Method in numbered steps** with times and visual signs, such as "fry until oil rises to the top".
**Critical points:** the steps that make or break the dish, such as reducing the base before frying.
**Storage and holding:** how long it keeps chilled, and how to reheat it.
The stew base: reduce before you fry

Fresh tomatoes are mostly water, roughly 94%. If you blend them and pour them straight into hot oil, the oil spits, the stew takes a long time to fry and the result can taste sour and raw. Professionals first **boil down** the blended tomato, tatashe (red bell pepper), scotch bonnet and onion until much of the water has gone. Then they fry the thick paste in oil until the oil separates and rises to the top. That sign means the water has cooked out and the sour, raw taste has gone.
Worked example: yield and cost of a stew base
For example, Ngozi in Owerri prepares stew base on Mondays for her weekday rice orders and wants to know her cost per portion.
She blends 5 kg tomatoes, 1 kg tatashe, 0.5 kg scotch bonnet and 1 kg onions. Total blended weight: 7.5 kg.
She boils it uncovered until it has halved, checking by weighing the pot (she knows the empty pot weight). Reduced weight: about 3.75 kg.
She fries it in 0.6 kg of vegetable oil with seasoning until the oil rises. She weighs the finished base: 4 kg.
Ingredient cost (approximate prices): tomatoes N12,000, tatashe N4,000, scotch bonnet N2,000, onions N2,500, oil N1,800, seasoning N700. Total N23,000.
At 120 g per plate: 4,000 g divided by 120 g = 33 portions. Cost per portion: N23,000 divided by 33 = about N697.
Ngozi now knows each plate carries about N697 of stew. She writes the weights on her recipe card so her assistant can repeat it exactly.

Layering flavour in soups

In soups, flavour is built in layers, and the order matters. For **egusi**, many professional cooks fry the ground melon in palm oil with a little onion, or drop it in as small lumps of paste and leave it to set before stirring, depending on whether the customer wants a fried or lumpy style. Both work; what matters is that you choose one style, write it down and always do it the same way.
**Base layer:** stock from the meats you cooked first. This is where the deep savoury taste comes from.
**Fat and aromatics:** palm oil, onion, locust beans (iru) or crayfish, cooked until fragrant.
**Body:** egusi, ogbono, cocoyam paste or blended vegetables that thicken the soup.
**Fresh layer last:** leafy vegetables such as ugwu, spinach (efo) or bitter leaf go in near the end so they stay green and keep more of their vitamins.
**Final check:** taste for salt, heat and sourness, then adjust in small steps.
Bleaching palm oil

Some cooks heat palm oil until it turns pale ("bleaching") for dishes such as ayamase. This produces heavy smoke and breaks down the oil. If you do it, use a small quantity, keep the heat moderate, stay with the pot, open doors and windows, and never let the oil catch fire. Many professional cooks prefer to buy refined palm oil or use green pepper sauce styles that do not need it.
Season in stages
Salt and seasoning cubes concentrate as soups reduce. Season lightly at the start, then adjust at the end. Write your final quantities on the recipe card.

Cooled stew base keeps well in a clean, covered container in the fridge for a few days, and much longer frozen in portion bags. Label each bag with the name, weight and date. Reheat only what you need, and bring it to a full simmer before serving.

Grains and legumes are the backbone of West African meals: rice, maize, millet, sorghum, acha (fonio), beans, soybeans and groundnuts. Cooking them well is a precision skill. Too much water gives mushy rice; too little gives hard grains and a burnt pot. In a business, the same mistake repeated over 100 portions is expensive.
A pile of beans
Beans and grains cook best when you measure water and soak or wash them correctly.
Rice and acha: measure the water

For white rice cooked by the **absorption method**, you add just enough water for the grains to soak up, cover the pot and cook gently until the water is gone. Parboiled long-grain rice, the type most sold in Nigeria, usually needs more water than raw white rice because the grain is harder. Washing rice until the water runs nearly clear removes surface starch and helps stop grains sticking. Ofada rice is often a little stony, so pick it over carefully before washing.

These are starting ratios. The right answer for your rice and your pot is the one you have tested and written down. When you scale up for a big pot, the water ratio stays roughly the same but less water evaporates per cup of rice, so reduce slightly and check.
Beans: soak, discard water, cook
**Sort.** Remove stones, damaged and insect-holed beans.
**Soak.** Cover with plenty of water and soak for 6 to 8 hours or overnight. Soaked beans cook noticeably faster, which saves gas.
**Discard the soaking water.** Some of the sugars that cause bloating dissolve into it.
**Cook in fresh water** until soft all the way through. Add salt near the end.
**For moi moi and akara,** soak briefly and rub off the skins, then blend to a smooth paste.
Chemicals on stored beans

Some traders spray stored beans and grains with insecticides to keep weevils away. NAFDAC has warned the public against using pesticides such as dichlorvos to preserve food. Buy from sellers you trust, reject beans with a chemical smell or powdery residue, and wash and soak beans well. Store your own beans in clean, airtight containers in a cool, dry place.
Worked example: testing a yield so you buy the right amount
For example, Amina in Abuja serves a beans and dodo lunch and wants to know how much dry beans she needs for 60 portions of 250 g cooked beans.
She soaks and cooks 1 kg of dry beans and weighs the cooked beans: 2.4 kg. Her yield factor is 2.4.
She needs 60 x 250 g = 15,000 g cooked beans.
Dry beans needed: 15,000 g divided by 2.4 = 6,250 g.
She adds about 5% for sorting losses: 6,250 x 1.05 = about 6,560 g, so she buys 6.5 to 7 kg.
She records the yield factor on her recipe card and re-tests if she changes bean variety.
Amina buys 7 kg of dry beans, enough for 60 full portions with a small margin, instead of guessing.
Proteins that work together

Proteins are built from amino acids. Cereals such as rice and maize are relatively low in one amino acid called lysine. Legumes such as beans and soybeans are richer in lysine but lower in methionine, which cereals supply better. Eating cereals and legumes together, as in rice and beans, moi moi with pap, or akara with bread, gives a better mix of amino acids than either alone. This is useful when animal protein is expensive.

Animal proteins such as eggs, fish, chicken and goat meat are complete proteins. Eggs are among the cheapest. Keep them cool and dry, use cracked eggs only in fully cooked dishes, and cook eggs for children, pregnant women and older people until the yolk is firm. Soybeans can be made into soy milk and "awara" (soy cheese), affordable proteins that many Nigerian families already enjoy.

People eat with their eyes first. Two plates of the same ofada rice and ayamase can earn very different reactions: one heaped untidily with sauce running over the rim, the other neat, colourful and generous. Presentation does not need expensive ingredients. It needs a plan, the right tools and clean habits.
A plate with a fork and knife

Five principles of a good plate

**Balance:** a clear main item, a starch and a vegetable or side. Think of the plate as a clock face: many chefs put the protein at the front (6 o'clock), the starch at the back left and the vegetables at the back right. Keep your layout the same for every plate.

**Colour contrast:** white rice next to green vegetables and red stew looks fresh. Brown food next to brown food looks dull. Add something green or bright, such as sliced cucumber, steamed carrots or fried plantain.
**Height:** a small mound of rice shaped in a bowl or ring mould gives the plate shape. Lean the protein against it.
**Space and clean rims:** leave the rim of the plate empty. Wipe drips with a clean, damp paper towel before serving.
**Sauce control:** spoon stew next to or over part of the protein, not across the whole plate, so the rice stays white and the plate stays clean.
Portion control tools

Portion scoops and ladles are sold by volume, for example a 125 ml or 250 ml ladle. When every plate is filled with the same tools, every customer gets the same amount and your costing stays accurate. Test each tool once: fill it with your rice or stew, weigh the contents, and write the weight on a strip of tape on the handle.

Garnish with purpose

Every garnish should be edible and belong to the dish: scent leaf on pepper soup, sliced spring onion on fried rice, a little fresh pepper on asun. Avoid inedible decorations or flowers you are not sure are safe to eat.
Hygiene while plating

Plating means a lot of hand contact with ready-to-eat food. Wash hands before starting, use tongs and spoons rather than fingers, and wear clean gloves if you must touch food, changing them if you touch money, phones or your face. Keep hot components covered and hot until they are plated, and plate in batches that can be served straight away.

For takeaway packs, the same principles apply. Put sauce in a separate small container or in a compartment so rice stays fluffy, line up the plantain neatly, and close the lid without pressing food against it. A clean sticker with your business name and the dish name finishes the look.

Nutrition Science for African Families

Good cooking feeds the body as well as pleasing the tongue. This module explains the three macronutrients and how to count energy from a food label, the vitamins and minerals most often lacking in West African diets, how to plan a week of family meals using WHO healthy diet guidance, and how to adapt cooking for family members living with diabetes or high blood pressure, always alongside their health worker's advice.

Every food is made of nutrients. Three of them, **carbohydrates, proteins and fats**, are needed in large amounts and provide energy, so they are called **macronutrients**. Vitamins and minerals are needed in tiny amounts and are called micronutrients; they are the subject of the next lesson. Understanding macronutrients lets you read a food label, judge a plate and plan meals with confidence.

Energy in food is measured in kilocalories (kcal), often just called calories. Notice that fat gives more than twice the energy of carbohydrate or protein per gram. That is why oily food is so filling, and why a few extra spoons of oil in every pot add up over a week.
Carbohydrates: quality matters
**Starches** in whole grains, yam, beans, plantain and cassava release energy steadily, especially with their fibre intact.
**Fibre** is a carbohydrate the body cannot digest. It keeps bowels regular and helps you feel full. Beans, vegetables, fruit, whole grains, ofada rice and unpolished grains are good sources.

**Free sugars** are sugars added to food and drinks, plus sugar in honey, syrups and fruit juice. WHO recommends keeping free sugars below 10% of daily energy, and suggests below 5% for further benefit. Soft drinks and sweetened malt drinks are a major source.

Processing changes carbohydrates. Polished white rice, white bread and garri have lost much of their fibre, so they are digested faster than ofada rice, whole maize or beans. You do not need to give up favourite staples. Serve them in sensible portions alongside beans and vegetables, which slow digestion and keep the family full for longer.
Worked example: reading a food label

For example, Grace in Lagos is checking the label on a pack of instant noodles she gives her children. The label says that one 70 g pack contains 45 g carbohydrate, 7 g protein and 14 g fat. (These are illustrative figures; always read your own label.)
Energy from carbohydrate: 45 g x 4 kcal = 180 kcal.
Energy from protein: 7 g x 4 kcal = 28 kcal.
Energy from fat: 14 g x 9 kcal = 126 kcal.
Total energy: 180 + 28 + 126 = 334 kcal.
Share from fat: 126 divided by 334 = 0.38, so about 38% of the energy comes from fat.
Grace sees that the pack is high in fat and low in protein. She adds an egg and some chopped vegetables to raise the protein and fibre and makes it an occasional food rather than daily.
Protein: how much is enough?

For healthy adults, the WHO, FAO and UN University expert report sets a safe level of protein intake of about 0.83 g of good quality protein per kilogram of body weight per day. A woman who weighs 65 kg therefore needs about 65 x 0.83 = 54 g of protein a day. Children, pregnant and breastfeeding women need relatively more for their size, so their health worker's guidance comes first. As a rough picture, 54 g could come from one egg, a portion of beans and a piece of fish over the day.
Fats: type and amount

WHO advises that total fat should be no more than about 30% of daily energy, saturated fat less than 10%, and industrially produced trans fats as low as possible. Trans fats are found in some baked and fried snacks made with partially hydrogenated oils. Palm oil is a valued traditional fat and rich in vitamin A in its red form, but it is high in saturated fat, so measure it rather than pouring freely. Use groundnut, soybean or other vegetable oils for some cooking, and get fats from whole foods like groundnuts and fish.

Measure your oil

Use a measuring spoon or a marked cup for oil when cooking for the family. One tablespoon of oil is roughly 13 to 14 g of fat, about 120 kcal. Cutting two tablespoons from a family pot removes about 240 kcal without changing the dish much.
Balance, not banning
No single food is good or bad on its own. Aim for a plate with a starch, a protein and plenty of vegetables, and keep sugary drinks and very oily snacks occasional.

When they are missing, the effects can be serious: tiredness and poor concentration from anaemia, night blindness and frequent infections from vitamin A deficiency, and poor growth in children. WHO describes iodine, vitamin A and iron deficiencies as among the most important worldwide, zinc deficiency is also common, and women of childbearing age and young children are most at risk.

Getting more iron out of your food

Iron in meat, fish and chicken (called **haem iron**) is absorbed well. Iron in beans, grains and vegetables (**non-haem iron**) is absorbed less well, but what you eat with it makes a big difference. Vitamin C in the same meal helps the body absorb non-haem iron. Tea and coffee contain compounds that reduce iron absorption when drunk with meals. Even a small piece of fish or meat in a bean dish improves absorption of the iron from the beans.

Worked example: improving a teenage daughter's meals

For example, Esther in Jos notices her 15-year-old daughter is often tired. The clinic has checked her and advised more iron-rich food. Her usual day is tea and bread in the morning, rice and stew at school, and garri with sugar in the evening.
Breakfast: Esther swaps tea for pap made with a spoon of ground crayfish or groundnut, plus a slice of pawpaw. Tea moves to mid-morning, at least an hour away from meals.
School lunch: she packs rice with beans instead of rice alone, and adds sliced tomato and cucumber.
Evening: three nights a week she cooks efo riro or ugwu soup with fish or a small piece of liver, served with an orange.
Weekly check: she plans liver or red meat at least once and beans at least three times, and writes it on the family meal plan.
Without buying expensive foods, the daughter now gets iron at every meal, with vitamin C alongside and tea away from meals. Esther keeps follow-up appointments as the clinic advised.
Cooking to keep vitamins
**Wash vegetables before cutting, not after.** Washing cut leaves rinses away water-soluble vitamins.
**Cook leafy vegetables briefly** and add them near the end of cooking.
**Use little water and cover the pot.** Vitamins leak into cooking water; use that water in the soup instead of pouring it away.
**Avoid adding potash (kaun) or baking soda** to keep vegetables green; alkalis destroy some vitamins, including vitamin C.
**Pair vitamin A foods with a little fat.** Vitamin A is fat-soluble, so a little oil in vegetable soup helps the body absorb it.
**Use iodised salt, stored covered** away from heat and sunlight, and add it towards the end of cooking.

Red palm oil deserves special mention. It is one of the richest local sources of beta-carotene, which the body turns into vitamin A. Very long, high heating destroys much of it, so soups cooked gently with red palm oil keep more of this value than oil that has been heated until pale. A little goes a long way.
Supplements need a health worker

Do not give iron, vitamin A or other supplements to children or adults on your own guesswork. Too much iron is poisonous to young children, and too much vitamin A is harmful, especially in pregnancy. In Nigeria, routine supplements such as iron and folic acid in pregnancy and vitamin A for young children are given through antenatal clinics and health facilities. Follow their advice and keep all supplements locked away from children.
Fermenting and soaking help
Soaking, sprouting and fermenting grains and legumes, as in ogi or iru, reduce phytates, natural compounds that bind iron and zinc. Traditional methods have real nutritional value.

If someone in your family shows signs such as constant tiredness, pale inner eyelids, breathlessness, or poor sight in dim light, take them to a health facility. Food helps prevent deficiencies, but diagnosis and treatment belong to health workers.

Families who plan meals usually eat better and spend less. Without a plan, the evening question "what are we eating?" leads to last-minute buying, the same three dishes repeated, and more noodles and soft drinks than anyone intended. A simple weekly plan fixes this in about 30 minutes a week.
A family eating together at a table
A weekly plan turns healthy eating into a family routine rather than a daily struggle.
The WHO healthy diet targets
**Fruit and vegetables:** at least 400 g a day for adults, about five portions. Starchy roots such as yam, cassava and potato do not count towards this.
**Salt:** less than 5 g a day for adults, which is just under one level teaspoon, and use iodised salt. Remember that seasoning cubes and salty snacks add salt too.
**Free sugars:** less than 10% of energy. In practice: water instead of soft drinks, and sweets and sugary drinks as treats.
**Fats:** prefer unsaturated oils, limit fried snacks and avoid industrially produced trans fats.
**Variety:** staples, legumes, vegetables, fruit and animal foods across the week.
Feeding babies and young children

WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months, then nutritious complementary foods from 6 months while breastfeeding continues up to 2 years or beyond. A baby's first foods should be soft and thick enough to stay on a spoon, such as pap enriched with groundnut paste or crayfish powder, mashed beans, or mashed yam with a little fish and oil. Do not add salt or sugar to a baby's food. Wash hands, bowls and spoons carefully, and give freshly prepared food.

**Fill a 7-day grid** for breakfast, lunch and dinner. Each day should include a legume or animal protein, at least two vegetable servings and one fruit.
**Plan cook-once, eat-twice meals:** a big pot of soup on Sunday serves Sunday and Tuesday; stew base made on Monday serves rice on Monday and beans on Wednesday.
**Write a shopping list by market section** with quantities, and check what you already have.
**Prepare ahead:** pick and wash vegetables, soak beans the night before, portion and freeze proteins.

Diabetes and high blood pressure (hypertension) are common in Nigerian families. Food is a central part of managing both. As the cook, you have real influence: the amount of salt, oil and sugar in the family pot, the size of the swallow portion, and how many vegetables reach the plate. This lesson shows practical changes. It does not replace medical care. Anyone with these conditions should follow their health worker's plan and take medicines exactly as prescribed.
A person living a healthy lifestyle

High blood pressure: the salt problem

Eating too much salt (sodium) raises blood pressure. WHO advises adults to eat less than 5 g of salt a day, just under one level teaspoon, and lowering salt is one of the most effective diet changes for people with hypertension. In many Nigerian kitchens, salt comes from three places: salt added in the pot, seasoning cubes, and salty foods such as some processed meats, snacks and salted fish. Eating more vegetables and fruit, which contain potassium, also helps, unless a health worker has advised limiting potassium, for example because of kidney disease.
Worked example: lowering the salt in a pot of soup
For example, Joy in Calabar cooks a pot of edikang ikong that serves 10 portions over two days. Her father has high blood pressure. She usually adds 3 level teaspoons of salt plus 4 seasoning cubes.
A level teaspoon of salt weighs roughly 5 g, so 3 teaspoons is about 15 g of added salt.
Per portion from added salt alone: 15 g divided by 10 = about 1.5 g, before counting the cubes, stockfish, periwinkle and other salty ingredients.
She cuts the salt to 1.5 teaspoons (about 7.5 g) and the cubes from 4 to 1. Added salt per portion falls to about 0.75 g plus a little from one cube.
She builds flavour instead with homemade stock, crayfish, a little iru, fresh pepper and plenty of vegetables.
She soaks dried fish and stockfish well to wash out some of the salt, and keeps the salt shaker off the table.

Bacteria, moulds and yeasts need water to grow. When you remove enough water from food, they cannot multiply, and the food keeps for months instead of days. Drying is one of the oldest preservation methods in Africa: think of dried okra, crayfish, stockfish and dried pepper. In this lesson you will use the same principle on products that fetch good prices in towns: dried tomato, dried ginger, mango slices and dried leafy vegetables.

**Leafy vegetables (ugwu, spinach, bitter leaf):** wash whole leaves, then **blanch** them: dip in boiling water for about 1 to 2 minutes and cool quickly in clean cold water. Blanching keeps colour and slows enzyme damage during drying.

Fermenting ogi and vegetables, and making vinegar pickles safely
Explain how lactic acid fermentation preserves food
Make ogi (akamu) from maize with clean, repeatable steps
Calculate salt for a fermented vegetable brine
Make quick vinegar pickles and know when a ferment must be discarded

Fermentation uses friendly microbes to change food. In **lactic acid fermentation**, bacteria naturally present on grains and vegetables turn sugars into lactic acid. The acid gives the sour taste of ogi, and it makes the food too acidic for many harmful bacteria to grow. West Africa has a rich fermentation tradition: ogi, iru and dawadawa, ugba, fufu, garri and kunu all depend on it.
A glass jar
Clean jars, the right salt or acid level and good hygiene make fermentation safe and repeatable.
Ogi (akamu) step by step
**Sort and wash** dry maize (or millet or sorghum for other types of ogi). Remove stones and mouldy grains.
**Steep** the grain in clean water in a covered container for 1 to 3 days, changing the water daily, until the grains are soft enough to crush with your fingers.
**Wet mill** the softened grain at a clean mill, or blend it in small batches with water.
**Sieve** through a fine cloth or mesh with plenty of clean water. The fibre (husk) stays behind; the starchy liquid passes through.
**Settle and sour:** leave the liquid covered for 1 to 3 days. The starch settles and sours. Pour off the water on top.
**Store** the wet ogi cake covered with a thin layer of clean water, changing it daily, or press it in a cloth bag. Keep it cool and use within a few days.
A typical ogi production week
Day 1: sort, wash, steep
Day 2 to 3: change water
Day 3: mill and sieve
Day 4 to 5: settle and sour
Day 5: drain, pack, sell
Planning the steps across the week lets you sell fresh ogi on fixed days.

Fresh ogi has a clean, pleasantly sour smell. Ogi that smells putrid, looks pink, grey or black, or has fuzzy mould must be thrown away. Sieving fibre removes some nutrients, so many families enrich pap with groundnut paste, crayfish powder or soy flour when they cook it, especially for children.
Salt-brined vegetables

Cabbage, carrots, cucumbers and garden eggs can be fermented in salt. Salt draws out juice, slows unwanted microbes and lets lactic acid bacteria take over. Too little salt and the vegetables go soft and smell bad; too much and fermentation stalls. Many tested recipes use about 2% to 2.5% salt by weight. Weigh the salt; spoons vary too much.
Worked example: salting a cabbage and carrot ferment
For example, Ruth in Jos wants to make a spicy fermented slaw to sell to two restaurants that serve grills.
She shreds 1,800 g of cabbage and 200 g of carrots: 2,000 g of vegetables in total.
At 2% salt: 2,000 g x 0.02 = 40 g of fine salt with no anti-caking additives.
She mixes and massages the salt in until juice comes out, adds sliced scotch bonnet and ginger, and packs it tightly into a clean jar so the juice covers the vegetables.
She weighs the vegetables down under the brine with a smaller clean jar filled with water, covers loosely and keeps it at room temperature out of the sun.
She tastes it from day 3. When it is pleasantly sour, about day 5 to 7 in warm weather, she moves it to the fridge.
Ruth has a repeatable recipe: 2% salt by weight, vegetables kept under the brine, refrigerated once sour. She records the date and taste each time.
Quick vinegar pickles

Vinegar pickles do not rely on fermentation. The acid from the vinegar preserves the vegetables directly. Use vinegar labelled 5% acidity, and follow a tested recipe for the vinegar to water ratio; do not dilute it more than the recipe says, because the acid level is what keeps the pickle safe. For a simple refrigerator pickle, pour hot brine of equal parts 5% vinegar and water, with salt and a little sugar, over sliced cucumber, onion or carrot in a clean jar, cool, and keep it in the fridge.
When to throw a ferment away

A thin white film on the surface of a brine is often a harmless yeast and can be skimmed, but fuzzy mould of any colour, a slimy texture, a rotten smell or pink, black or grey patches mean the batch must be discarded. Never taste a ferment that smells bad. Use only clean water, clean jars and clean hands. Low-acid foods such as plain vegetables in oil are not made safe by this method.
Check acidity with pH strips

Cheap pH test strips let you check that a ferment or pickle has become acidic. Food safety guidance treats a pH of 4.6 or below as the line below which botulism bacteria cannot grow; well-made pickles usually measure lower.

This module turns your cooking skills into a business that runs smoothly and legally. Cooking well is only half of event catering. The other half is **operations**: getting the right food, people and equipment to the right place, serving every guest within a reasonable time, and leaving the venue clean. Many caterers lose clients not because the food was poor, but because the queue was long, food ran out on one side of the hall, or servers did not know what to do.

Staffing rules of thumb

Caterers use rough guides and then adjust for the venue and the client. Patience quotes for 17 staff and 17 chafing dishes instead of guessing, briefs each person on their station, and her team serves 280 buffet guests in good time.

**Cooking:** burners, pots with lids, gas cylinders, regulators and hoses, cooking spoons, chopping boards in separate colours for raw and cooked food.
**Holding and service:** chafing dishes with fuel, insulated food flasks or coolers, serving spoons and tongs (one per dish), food probe thermometer.
**Hygiene:** handwashing station with soap and clean water, paper towels, gloves, hair covers, aprons, refuse bags, cleaning cloths and sanitiser.

Timing is the main food safety tool at events. Cook as close to service as you can, transport hot food in insulated flasks or covered pots that are full and tightly closed, and check the temperature on arrival with your probe thermometer. Hot food should stay above 60 C during service. Light chafing dish fuel 15 to 20 minutes before the lines open so the water underneath is already hot, and top up dishes with fresh hot food rather than mixing new food into old.

Agree with the client in advance what happens to leftovers. Food that has stood on a buffet for hours should not be packed for guests to take home. Throw away anything that has been out of temperature control for more than 2 hours.

A **run sheet** is a timed list of what happens and who does it: when the van leaves, when the team arrives, when lines open, when the cake is cut, when service closes and when the team must leave the hall. Share it on your team WhatsApp group the day before and print one copy for the supervisor.

If you smell gas, turn off the cylinder valve, put out all flames, do not switch electrical items on or off, and move people away. Keep a fire extinguisher and a fire blanket at the cooking area.

Before the event, check where you will cook, where water and power points are, how far the kitchen is from the hall, and what time you can enter. Many day-of problems are solved by a 20-minute venue visit.

**Dog:** unpopular and low margin. Remove it, or redesign it completely.

Professional cooks get the same result every time because they understand what heat, water, fat and time do to food.
Seasoning cubes are quick, but they add a lot of salt and every pot tastes the same. Stock lets you control the salt.
Goat meat, cow leg and oxtail are full of flavour. The right method makes them soft enough to pull apart.

Step by step
Cool stock in shallow containers; fridge within 2 hours.
Bones with connective tissue, in cold water
Skim the grey foam

Simmer gently, never a hard boil
No salt; strain, label and chill
Step one. Use bones with connective tissue, like chicken backs, necks and feet. Start them in cold water, covering the bones by about 5 cm.
Step two. As it heats, skim off the grey foam.
Step three. Add aromatics, about one tenth of the bone weight: onion, garlic, ginger and thyme.
Step four. Keep it at a gentle simmer, with small bubbles just breaking the surface. The common mistake is a hard boil, which makes stock cloudy and greasy.
Step five. Do not salt the stock. Season the final dish instead.
Bacteria grow fastest between about 5 C and 60 C. So divide hot stock into shallow containers, stand them in cold water, and refrigerate within 2 hours. Never leave stock on the stove overnight.

Pat meat dry, then sear in batches
Liquid half to two thirds up the meat
Cover and keep a lazy simmer
Judge by texture, not the clock
Plan backwards from serving time
Tough cuts are rich in collagen. Long, gentle, moist heat melts it into gelatin. First pat the meat dry, because wet meat steams instead of browning. Sear it in batches without crowding.
Add stock until it reaches about half to two thirds of the way up the meat.
Cover and keep only occasional bubbles. A hard boil gives dry, stringy meat.
Goat meat often needs 1.5 to 2.5 hours, and cow leg 2.5 to 4 hours. But a fork sliding in easily is the real test.
For example, Halima in Kano wants goat meat for 12 ready at 1:00 pm. She works backwards through margin, sauce, braising and searing, and starts at 9:30 am.

Do
Pat the surface dry
Leave space between pieces
Probe the thickest part: 70 C
Never
Guess by colour alone

Put cooked suya on the raw plate

The WHO Five Keys to Safer Food advise cooking food until it reaches 70 C. Probe the thickest part, away from the bone, then rest the meat.
Clear juices are helpful signs, but they are not proof.
Charcoal gives off carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell that can kill. Never grill inside a room, kitchen or garage, even with a window open. And keep raw and cooked trays separate.

Most frying works at about 160 to 180 C. Fry small batches, golden not dark brown.
Oil no more than one third of the pot. Handle turned in. Never leave hot oil alone.
Never use water. Turn off the gas, slide a lid or damp fire blanket over it. Do not carry it.
Oil that is too cool soaks into food. Oil that is too hot burns the outside first. Most frying works best at about 160 to 180 C.
Fry small batches, and fry yam, potato and plantain to golden, not dark brown.
Never fill a pot more than about one third with oil. Keep the handle turned in, lower food gently, keep children away, and never leave hot oil, even for a phone call.

If oil catches fire, never pour water on it. It throws flaming oil across the room. Turn off the gas if you can reach it safely, slide a metal lid or a damp fire blanket over the pot, and leave it covered until cool.

Why this matters

Preserving food lets you buy produce when it is cheap.
It cuts waste when the market is full of tomatoes or mango.
And it creates products like dried tomato, ogi, pickles, yaji and pepper sauce that sell between events.
The secret is consistency. The hundredth jar must taste exactly like the first, and every one must be safe.
Drying
Mould means discard the whole batch. Never pick it out.
Sort, wash and slice evenly, 6 to 8 mm
Blanch leafy greens; dip mango in lemon water
Dry in single layers in a covered solar dryer
Test: vegetables snap, fruit is leathery
Cool, pack airtight, label and date
Microbes need water to grow, so removing water makes food keep for months. Step one. Sort, wash and slice evenly, about 6 to 8 mm thick, so pieces dry at the same speed.
Step two. Blanch leafy vegetables in boiling water for about 1 to 2 minutes, then cool them quickly. Dip mango in diluted lemon juice to limit browning.
Step three. Dry in single layers on clean mesh trays in a covered solar dryer, not on the ground or by the roadside.
Step four. Test it. Vegetables and ginger should snap. Mango should be leathery with no moisture when you tear and squeeze it.
Step five. Cool before packing. Warm food packed in a bag sweats and goes mouldy. Pack airtight, label and date it.
Throw away any batch with visible mould or a musty smell. Some moulds produce toxins you cannot see or remove.
Fermenting
Ogi and salt-brined vegetables
Ogi: steep 1 to 3 days, change water daily
Mill, sieve, then settle and sour
Brine: weigh salt at about 2% of vegetables
Keep vegetables under the brine
Vinegar pickles: 5% acidity, tested ratio
In fermentation, friendly bacteria turn sugars into acid, which keeps harmful bacteria away. For ogi, steep clean maize for 1 to 3 days, changing the water daily.
Mill it, sieve it with clean water, then let the starch settle and sour. Keep it cool and use within a few days.
For brined vegetables, weigh the salt. For example, Ruth in Jos used 2,000 g of cabbage and carrots, so 2,000 times 0.02 gives 40 g of salt. Spoons vary too much.
Pack tightly and keep the vegetables under the brine. When it tastes pleasantly sour, move it to the fridge.
Vinegar pickles need vinegar labelled 5% acidity. Never dilute it more than the tested recipe says, because the acid keeps it safe.
Safe or spoiled?
Usually fine
Clean, pleasantly sour smell
Thin white film: skim it
Discard
Fuzzy mould of any colour
Pink, grey or black patches
Slimy texture
Rotten or putrid smell
Fresh ogi and good ferments have a clean, pleasantly sour smell. A thin white film on brine is often a harmless yeast and can be skimmed.
But fuzzy mould of any colour, pink, grey or black patches, a slimy texture or a rotten smell mean the whole batch goes. Never taste a ferment that smells bad.

At least one supervisor who does not serve
A timed run sheet shared the day before
For plated service, plan about one server for every 10 to 15 guests.
At a staffed buffet, about one server for every 25 to 30 guests.

Plan one buffet line for every 75 to 100 guests, served from both sides if possible. For example, Patience in Uyo set 3 double-sided lines for 280 buffet guests, and quoted for 17 staff instead of guessing.

Safety at venues
Gas and hot food
Cylinders upright, ventilated, away from flames and guests. Check for leaks with soapy water.
Turn off the valve, put out all flames, do not switch electrics on or off, move people away.
Above 60 C during service. Discard food out of temperature control for more than 2 hours.
Keep gas cylinders upright, outdoors or well ventilated, away from the flame and from guests. Check hoses and connections with soapy water. Bubbles mean a leak. Never use a lighter to check.
Keep a fire extinguisher and fire blanket at the cooking area.
If you smell gas, turn off the cylinder valve, put out all flames, do not switch electrical items on or off, and move people away.
Hot food should stay above 60 C during service. Check it with your probe thermometer on arrival. Throw away anything out of temperature control for more than 2 hours.
Costing
Yield: you do not serve all you buy
Weight to buy = portion needed ÷ yield
Weigh what you buy (as purchased)
Trim, cook and weigh what you serve
Yield % = served ÷ bought × 100
Record your own yields; retest often
When you buy yam, plantain or fish, peel, bones and trimmings are lost. First, weigh what you buy. That is the as purchased weight.
Then trim, cook and weigh what you can actually serve. That is the edible portion.
Divide edible by purchased and multiply by 100 to get your yield percentage.
Your figures will change with season and supplier, so test your main ingredients yourself.
Then divide the portion you need by the yield. For example, 200 g of fried yam at 80% yield means buying 250 g.

Popular

Contribution margin is selling price minus food cost. Sort every dish by how many sold and by its margin.
A star is popular with a high margin, so keep it exactly the same. A plowhorse is popular with a low margin. Raise the price slightly or cut a costly component.

A puzzle has a high margin but few sales, so photograph it better and recommend it. A dog is unpopular and low margin. Remove or redesign it. Repeat this every month or two, because prices change quickly.

Use a written agreement for every event, and never claim a food cures anything.
